name: The Renaissance
line: Look closely, draw what you see, read the old books and try your hand at everything.

quote.text: A man can do all things if he will.
quote.source: The saying by which he was remembered, as given by Jacob Burckhardt in 1860 from an anonymous fifteenth-century life

quotes.text: All our knowledge has its origin in our perceptions.
quotes.source: Notebooks, Codex Trivulzianus, folio 20 verso; translated by Jean Paul Richter, 1883

quotes.text: Thou mayest fashion thyself in whatever shape thou shalt prefer.
quotes.source: God speaking to Adam in the Oration on the Dignity of Man, 1486; translated by Elizabeth Livermore Forbes

quotes.text: I enter the ancient courts of ancient men, where, received by them with affection, I feed on that food which only is mine.
quotes.source: Letter to Francesco Vettori, 10 December 1513, on his evenings of reading in exile
Ancora imparo. An older motto, found on a sixteenth-century print of an old man in a child’s walker; its link to Michelangelo is tradition

quotes.text: Practise in all things a certain nonchalance which conceals all artistry and makes whatever one says or does seem uncontrived and effortless.
quotes.source: The Book of the Courtier, 1528, book 1, chapter 26; translated by George Bull
Treatise on Painting, compiled from his notes after his death, opening section

quotes.text: Men go to admire the heights of mountains and the mighty waves of the sea, and pass themselves by.
quotes.source: Confessions, book 10, abridged. Petrarch tells how he opened the book at this passage on the summit of Mont Ventoux in 1336

words.usage: Giorgio Vasari’s word in 1550 for the revival of the arts since Giotto. The French form, renaissance, became the name of the age only in the nineteenth century.
Student slang for a teacher of the humanities: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy.
The curriculum of the humanists, built on the reading of Latin and Greek authors. The origin of the humanities.
The humanists’ rule: go behind the commentaries to the original text, in the original language.
Not virtue in the moral sense. The skill and energy with which a person meets circumstances and makes something of them.
The power of chance, pictured as a woman with a wheel. Machiavelli gave her half of human affairs and left the other half to us.
A person accomplished in every field, in body and in mind. Alberti and Leonardo are the models.
The natural gift that no training supplies. The root of engineer and of ingenious.
Both the line on the paper and the idea in the mind. Florentines held it to be the father of painting, sculpture and architecture.
A master’s shop, where apprentices from the age of twelve or so ground colours, prepared panels and learned by copying.
The lowest rank in the workshop, who swept, ran errands and drew when he could.
The head of a workshop, who signed the contracts and painted the faces.
The geometry by which depth is shown on a flat surface, with lines that meet at a vanishing point. Brunelleschi demonstrated it around 1415.
Modelling forms by shadow so that they look round.
Leonardo’s way of blending tones without lines or edges, like smoke.
A standing pose with the weight on one leg, so that hips and shoulders tilt opposite ways. Taken from ancient statues.
Painting on wet plaster, which binds the colour into the wall. Each day’s patch must be finished before it dries.
Pigment bound with egg yolk, the usual medium on panel until oil took over.
A drawing on heavy paper made to transfer a design to a wall or panel.

words.meaning: A heap of things; a commonplace book
words.usage: A notebook into which a Florentine merchant copied poems, recipes, sums, prayers and anything worth keeping.
Castiglione’s word of 1528 for the art of making what is difficult look effortless.
The ideal gentleman or lady of a court: armed, lettered, musical, witty and graceful.
From Maecenas, the friend of Virgil. Almost every work of the age was made to order for one.
In Florence, the nine citizens chosen by lot from the guilds to govern for two months at a time.
A general who hired out his army by contract. Some became princes and patrons.
A small private room for reading and thinking, lined with books, instruments and pictures.
The humanist theme that a person is free to rise or fall by their own choice.
Free time well spent on books and conversation, as opposed to negotium, business.
The debate over which art is nobler: painting or sculpture, the eye or the ear.
Works left rough, like Michelangelo’s figures half emerged from the block. Leonardo finished perhaps fifteen paintings.

practices.name: Draw from life
practices.instructions: Take a pencil and plain paper and draw one real thing in front of you for twenty minutes: your own hand, a folded cloth, a plant, a face. Do not draw what you know is there. Look for longer than you draw, and put down only what you see: the angle of this edge, where the shadow stops. Do not rub out. Date the sheet and keep it.
practices.why: Every Renaissance workshop began with drawing. Cennino Cennini’s handbook, written around 1400, tells the apprentice to draw every day without fail, however little. Leonardo filled thousands of pages with studies of hands, water, muscles and plants, convinced that drawing was a way of finding out how things are made.
variations: Copy a drawing by a master, line for line, as apprentices did.
Draw the same object every day for a week.
Draw a drapery study from a cloth dipped in plaster or simply pinned up.

practices.name: Keep a notebook like Leonardo
practices.instructions: Carry a small notebook all day. In the morning write a list of things you want to find out, as plainly as he did: how a bird holds still in wind, why the sky is blue, ask the mason how the wall is built. During the day write and sketch what you notice. Put everything in one book: sums, shopping, ideas, things overheard. Tomorrow, answer one item on the list by looking or by asking someone who knows.
practices.why: About seven thousand pages of Leonardo’s notebooks survive. They mix anatomy, engineering, grocery lists, jokes and drafts of letters, and they are full of notes to himself such as describe the tongue of the woodpecker. Florentine merchants kept similar books of everything worth remembering, which they called a zibaldone.
variations: Write a to-find-out list of ten items.
Try a line of mirror writing, right to left, as he wrote.
Ask an expert in any trade to show you one thing.

practices.name: Converse with the ancients
practices.instructions: Before you sit down, wash your face and change out of your working clothes. Then read for thirty minutes from an author who has been dead for at least five hundred years: Cicero, Seneca, Plutarch, Plato, Virgil, Dante. Read the text itself, not a summary. Read with a pen. When something strikes you, copy it into your notebook and write beneath it what you would ask the author if you could.
practices.why: The humanists believed that the best minds of Greece and Rome could be spoken with directly through their books. Petrarch wrote letters to Cicero. Machiavelli, banished to his farm, described how each evening he took off his muddy clothes, put on the robes of court and spent four hours with the ancients, asking them the reasons for their actions.
variations: Read a page with the original language on the facing side.
Write a letter to a dead author.
Learn ten lines of a poem by heart.

practices.name: Train the whole person
practices.instructions: Spend half an hour on whichever side of yourself you have neglected. If you live in your head, do something with your body: run, swim, wrestle, ride, dance, lift. If you live in your body, sing, play an instrument, work a problem in geometry or write verse. Whatever you choose, work at it until it begins to look easy, and do not complain about the effort.
practices.why: The age admired those who could do everything. Alberti was architect, author, athlete and musician, and was said to jump over a standing man with his feet together. Castiglione’s courtier had to ride, fence, swim, dance, draw, sing to the lute and speak well, and to do it all with an ease that hid the labour.
variations: Learn the first steps of a dance.
Take up an instrument for the month.
Practise one skill until you can do it without showing strain.

practices.name: An hour in the study
practices.instructions: Make one small place your study: a desk, a corner, a chair by a lamp. Put in it only what helps you think: a few books, your notebook, one beautiful object. Sit there for fifteen minutes at the end of the day with no screen. Look back through today’s notes. Finish one small thing you began, or decide plainly to leave it. Write tomorrow’s list of things to find out.
practices.why: Scholars and princes built themselves a studiolo, a small private room for study. The duke of Urbino lined his with pictures of books, instruments and a squirrel made in inlaid wood, under portraits of great thinkers. Jerome in his study was among the most painted subjects of the century.
variations: Tidy your desk as if a painter were coming to paint it.
Choose one portrait of someone you admire to hang above it.
Spend the time in conversation with a friend, as the academies did.

tasks.name: Read a chapter of The Lives of the Artists
tasks.meta: Read · Giorgio Vasari, 1550; try the life of Brunelleschi

tasks.name: Listen to the Missa Pange lingua
Look for ten minutes at The School of Athens
tasks.meta: Art · Raphael, 1509 to 1511; find the vanishing point

tasks.name: Play a game of chess
tasks.meta: Games · the modern queen dates from about 1475

tasks.name: Journal: what did you see today that you had looked at for years?
How much of your life is fortune, and how much is yours?
Ask someone who knows how a thing is made
Measure something and work out its proportions
Do one hard thing today as if it cost you nothing
Sketch your own hand for five minutes
Write a line in mirror writing
Look at a building and find its symmetry
Learn one new word in Latin or Italian and use it

rules.why: Trust your eyes before the textbook. Experience is the teacher of those who teach.
Even a little. The hand teaches the eye to see.
Read the original and not the commentary on it.
Body and mind, art and number. A person is not one trade.
Work hard in private and carry the result lightly in company.
However old or skilled, keep a list of what you do not know.

read.title: The Lives of the Artists
read.creator: Giorgio Vasari
read.why: Lives of the painters, sculptors and architects from Cimabue to Michelangelo, by a painter who knew many of them. Gossipy, partial to Florence and the founding book of art history.

read.title: The Book of the Courtier
read.creator: Baldassare Castiglione
read.why: Four evenings of conversation at the court of Urbino on what makes the perfect gentleman and lady.

read.title: The Prince
read.creator: Niccolò Machiavelli
read.why: A short and cold handbook on how power is won and kept, written by an out-of-office civil servant hoping for a job.

read.title: Oration on the Dignity of Man
read.creator: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
read.why: A speech by a twenty-three-year-old to introduce nine hundred theses he offered to defend against all comers.

read.title: Leonardo da Vinci
read.creator: Walter Isaacson
read.why: A life built from the notebooks, showing how the painting and the science fed each other.

read.title: The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy
read.creator: Jacob Burckhardt
read.why: The book that formed the idea of the Renaissance as the birth of the modern individual. Still worth arguing with.

watch.title: Civilisation, episodes 4 and 5
watch.creator: Kenneth Clark for the BBC
watch.why: Man the Measure of All Things and The Hero as Artist. A personal tour from Urbino to the Sistine Chapel.

watch.title: The Agony and the Ecstasy
watch.creator: Carol Reed
watch.why: Michelangelo and Pope Julius II quarrel their way through four years of the Sistine ceiling.

watch.title: Medici: Godfathers of the Renaissance
watch.creator: Justin Hardy for PBS
watch.why: Four hours on the banking family that ran Florence and paid for much of its art.

watch.title: Leonardo: The Works
watch.creator: Phil Grabsky, Exhibition on Screen
watch.why: Every painting attributed to Leonardo, filmed slowly and in close detail for the five hundredth anniversary of his death.

listen.title: Missa Pange lingua
listen.creator: Josquin des Prez
listen.why: A late mass for four voices in which each line grows from a plainchant hymn. Luther called him the master of the notes.

listen.title: Nuper rosarum flores
listen.creator: Guillaume Dufay
listen.why: Written for the consecration of Florence Cathedral under Brunelleschi’s new dome.

listen.title: Missa Papae Marcelli
listen.creator: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
listen.why: Six voices in clear and serene polyphony, long said to have saved church music at the Council of Trent.

listen.title: L’Orfeo
listen.creator: Claudio Monteverdi
listen.why: The first great opera, made at Mantua by musicians trying to revive Greek tragedy.

art.title: The School of Athens
art.creator: Raphael
art.why: Plato and Aristotle walk through a vast hall among the philosophers of antiquity, several with the faces of Raphael’s contemporaries. In the Vatican.

art.title: Primavera
art.creator: Sandro Botticelli
art.why: Venus, the Graces, Mercury and Flora in an orange grove with some five hundred kinds of plant. In the Uffizi, Florence.

art.title: The Holy Trinity
art.creator: Masaccio
art.why: A painted chapel that seems to open into the wall of the church. The first full use of mathematical perspective. In Santa Maria Novella, Florence.

art.title: David
art.creator: Michelangelo
art.why: Seventeen feet of marble carved by a man of twenty-six from a block others had abandoned. In the Accademia, Florence.

art.title: The Vitruvian Man
art.creator: Leonardo da Vinci
art.why: A man in a circle and a square, after the Roman architect’s rule of proportion. In the Accademia, Venice.

eat.title: Ribollita
eat.creator: Reboiled bread and bean soup with black cabbage
eat.why: Tuscan thrift. Yesterday’s soup cooked again with stale bread.

eat.title: Pici with garlic
eat.creator: Thick hand-rolled pasta
eat.why: Flour and water rolled between the palms, as in the countryside around Siena.

eat.title: Panforte
eat.creator: A dense cake of honey, nuts and spice
eat.why: Made in Siena since the Middle Ages with pepper and other costly spices.

eat.title: Roast meat with rosemary
eat.creator: Cooked on the spit
eat.why: Leonardo’s notebooks include a design for a roasting spit turned by the rising heat of its own fire.

drink.title: Red wine of Tuscany
drink.creator: Sangiovese
drink.why: Machiavelli grew and sold it from his farm at Sant’Andrea in Percussina, where the estate still makes wine.

drink.title: Watered wine
drink.creator: Wine cut with water
drink.why: The everyday drink at table for all ages.

drink.title: Vin santo
drink.creator: Sweet amber wine
drink.why: Made from dried grapes and served with hard almond biscuits for dipping.

customs.title: The commonplace book
customs.creator: Copying out what is worth keeping
customs.why: Schoolboys were taught to keep a notebook of passages under headings, to be drawn on in their own writing.

customs.title: The evening walk
customs.creator: The passeggiata
customs.why: Before supper Italians still walk slowly through the main street or square to see and be seen.

customs.title: The competition
customs.creator: Art by contest
customs.why: Florence awarded its great commissions by public competition. Ghiberti beat Brunelleschi for the Baptistery doors in 1401.

customs.title: The academy
customs.creator: Friends who meet to talk
customs.why: Marsilio Ficino gathered a circle at a Medici villa to read Plato together and kept a lamp burning before his bust.

games.title: Chess
games.creator: Board game · Europe
games.why: In the late fifteenth century the queen and bishop gained their long moves and the game became fast. Castiglione thought a courtier should play it, but not too well.

games.title: Tarocchi
games.creator: Card game · northern Italy
games.why: A trick-taking game with an extra suit of picture trumps, painted for the dukes of Milan. Fortune-telling came three centuries later.

games.title: Calcio storico
games.creator: Ball game · Florence
games.why: Twenty-seven a side in a sand-covered square, part football and part brawl. It is still played each June in costume.

games.title: Pallone
games.creator: Ball game · Italy
games.why: A heavy ball struck with a spiked wooden sleeve on the forearm, played against town walls.

festivals.title: The feast of Saint John
festivals.creator: 24 June, Florence
festivals.why: The patron’s day, with the final of the historic football in Piazza Santa Croce and fireworks over the Arno.

festivals.title: The Palio
festivals.creator: 2 July and 16 August, Siena
festivals.why: Ten of the city’s districts race bareback three times round the shell-shaped square, as they have since the Middle Ages.

festivals.title: Carnival
festivals.creator: The days before Lent, Venice
festivals.why: Masks and disguise in the squares. Lorenzo de’ Medici wrote songs for the Florentine carnival floats.

festivals.title: The Explosion of the Cart
festivals.creator: Easter Sunday, Florence
festivals.why: A tall cart is drawn by white oxen to the cathedral and set off with fireworks lit by a dove-shaped rocket from the altar.

places.title: Florence Cathedral
places.creator: Florence, Italy
places.why: Brunelleschi’s dome of 1420 to 1436, built without scaffolding from the ground and still the largest brick dome in the world. Climb between its two shells.

places.title: The Uffizi
places.creator: Florence, Italy
places.why: The Medici offices turned gallery, with Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael in sequence.

places.title: The Ducal Palace
places.creator: Urbino, Italy
places.why: The hilltop court of Federico da Montefeltro, with his inlaid study and the rooms where the Courtier is set.

places.title: The Vatican Museums
places.creator: Rome
places.why: Raphael’s rooms and Michelangelo’s Sistine ceiling and Last Judgment.

places.title: Santa Maria delle Grazie
places.creator: Milan, Italy
places.why: Leonardo’s Last Supper on the wall of the friars’ dining room, painted in an experimental technique that began to flake in his lifetime.

places.title: Clos Lucé
places.creator: Amboise, France
places.why: The small manor where Leonardo spent his last three years as guest of the king of France, with models of his machines in the garden.

ethics.title: Curiosity
ethics.text: The desire to know is the mark of a good mind.
ethics.practice: Find out today the answer to one question you have carried for years.

ethics.title: Diligence
ethics.text: Talent is completed by daily practice.
ethics.practice: Do your twenty minutes of drawing whether you feel like it or not.

ethics.title: Dignity
ethics.text: Each person is free to make something of themselves.
ethics.practice: Treat someone today as capable of more than their position suggests.

ethics.title: Civic duty
ethics.text: Learning is for the service of one’s city.
ethics.practice: Use something you know for the good of the place you live.

ethics.title: Grace
ethics.text: Carry your skill lightly, without display.
ethics.practice: Let someone else take the credit for something.

ethics.title: Generosity to the arts
ethics.text: Wealth is well spent on beauty that all may see.
ethics.practice: Pay an artist, a musician or a maker for their work today.

philosophy.title: The dignity of man
philosophy.text: Pico imagined God telling Adam that he alone has no fixed nature and may make himself beast or angel.
philosophy.practice: What are you making of yourself?

philosophy.title: Fortune and virtù
philosophy.text: Machiavelli compared fortune to a river in flood. It cannot be stopped, and it can be prepared for with dykes.
philosophy.practice: What dyke should you be building now?

philosophy.title: Experience before authority
philosophy.text: Leonardo called himself a disciple of experience and distrusted those who only quoted books.
philosophy.practice: What do you believe only because you were told?

philosophy.title: The active and the contemplative life
philosophy.text: Humanists argued over whether it is better to study or to serve the city. Most said both.

philosophy.title: Man the measure
philosophy.text: Proportions of buildings were taken from the human body, and the human view was put at the centre of the picture.
philosophy.practice: What in your surroundings is out of human scale?

philosophy.title: Imitation and invention
philosophy.text: Artists learned by copying the ancients closely, so as to surpass them.
philosophy.practice: Whom are you copying on the way to your own manner?

philosophy.title: Is it better to be loved or feared
philosophy.text: Machiavelli answered that for a ruler it is safer to be feared, if he cannot be both, so long as he avoids being hated.
philosophy.practice: Is he right about anything in your own life?

philosophy.title: The unfinished
philosophy.text: Leonardo left most of what he began. Perfection kept him from completion.
philosophy.practice: What are you refusing to finish?

intro: In the fourteenth century the cities of northern Italy were the richest in Europe. Florence, Venice, Milan and Genoa lived by trade, cloth and banking, governed themselves and competed fiercely with one another. Their citizens were surrounded by the ruins of ancient Rome and spoke a language descended from Latin. Out of that setting came a movement that looked back past the preceding centuries to the Greeks and Romans, and by studying them changed what Europeans thought a human being could do.

It began with books. The poet Petrarch, who died in 1374, hunted through monastery libraries for lost works of Cicero and wrote letters to him as to a friend. Those who followed him were called humanists, after the humanities they taught: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy, studied from the original texts. They learned Greek from scholars who came from Constantinople, corrected corrupt manuscripts and exposed forgeries. They held that such an education made a person eloquent, wise and useful to the city. After 1450 the printing press spread their editions across the continent.

The same turn toward the ancient and the observed transformed the arts. In Florence in the 1420s the architect Brunelleschi raised a dome over the cathedral that no one had known how to build and worked out the rules of perspective. The sculptor Donatello made the first free-standing nude since antiquity. The painter Masaccio gave his figures weight and shadow. Artists studied anatomy, geometry and optics, and a trade that had been counted among the manual crafts began to claim a place among the liberal arts.

All of this was paid for by patrons. Guilds, popes, princes and bankers such as the Medici competed for the best artists as a matter of honour and policy. Works were made to contract in busy workshops where boys began as apprentices at twelve or thirteen. Leonardo trained in the shop of Verrocchio, and Michelangelo in that of Ghirlandaio.

Around 1500 the movement reached its height in the work of three men: Leonardo da Vinci, painter, engineer and student of everything; Michelangelo, sculptor of the David and painter of the Sistine ceiling; and Raphael, whose frescoes in the Vatican gave the age its image of calm perfection. In the same years Machiavelli wrote about politics as it is and not as it ought to be, and Castiglione described the ideal courtier. The sack of Rome by imperial troops in 1527 is often taken as the end of the High Renaissance, though its methods spread north to Dürer, Erasmus, Montaigne and Shakespeare.

The picture of a sudden dawn after a dark age was the Renaissance’s own advertisement, and historians no longer accept it. The Middle Ages had their own learning, and much was owed to Arab and Byzantine scholars who had kept Greek science alive. The age was violent, and its opportunities were open to few.
This Onda takes its practices from the habits of its artists and scholars: drawing from life, the notebook, reading the ancients, training body and mind together, and an hour in the study.
guide.origin: The cities of northern and central Italy, above all Florence, and later the rest of Europe
guide.era: From Petrarch in the mid-fourteenth century to about 1600. The High Renaissance of Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael falls between about 1490 and 1527

figures.name: Francesco Petrarca, called Petrarch
figures.bio: Poet and scholar from Arezzo, crowned laureate in Rome in 1341. His recovery of Cicero’s letters and his Italian sonnets made him the father of humanism.

figures.name: Filippo Brunelleschi
figures.bio: A goldsmith who lost the competition for the Baptistery doors, went to Rome to measure ruins, and came back to build the dome.

figures.name: Leon Battista Alberti
figures.bio: Architect, athlete and author of the first modern treatises on painting, building and the family. The original universal man.

figures.name: Lorenzo de' Medici
figures.bio: Banker, poet and unofficial ruler of Florence, called the Magnificent. He kept Botticelli and the young Michelangelo in his household.

figures.name: Leonardo da Vinci
figures.bio: The illegitimate son of a notary from a village near Florence. He painted the Last Supper and the Mona Lisa, dissected some thirty bodies and designed machines that were never built.

figures.name: Isabella d'Este
figures.bio: Marchioness of Mantua, who governed the state in her husband’s absence and was the most demanding collector of her time. Her study and letters survive.

figures.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
figures.bio: Sculptor, painter, architect and poet. He thought of himself as a carver and worked until six days before his death at eighty-eight.

figures.name: Raphael
figures.bio: Raffaello Sanzio of Urbino. Charming and prolific, he ran the largest workshop in Rome and died at thirty-seven.

figures.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
figures.bio: Secretary to the Florentine republic for fourteen years, then dismissed, tortured and sent to his farm, where he wrote.

figures.name: Sofonisba Anguissola
figures.bio: A nobleman’s daughter from Cremona who became court painter to the queen of Spain. Michelangelo praised her drawing, and Van Dyck visited her when she was past ninety.

figures.name: Vittoria Colonna
figures.bio: The most admired poet of her generation and Michelangelo’s closest friend, to whom he wrote sonnets and gave drawings.

figures.name: Giorgio Vasari
figures.bio: Painter and architect of the Uffizi, remembered for his book of artists’ lives.

history.detail: The poet receives the laurel on the Capitol in Rome, in a ceremony revived from antiquity.
Manuel Chrysoloras arrives from Constantinople to teach Greek in Florence. The Medici bank is founded in the same year.
Seven sculptors submit bronze panels of the sacrifice of Isaac. Ghiberti wins and spends the next fifty years on two sets of doors.
Brunelleschi vaults the cathedral with a double shell of brick laid in a herringbone pattern, using hoists of his own invention.
The banker returns from exile and governs Florence from behind the scenes for thirty years, spending a fortune on building and books.
Alberti writes down the rules of perspective and declares that the painter must be a learned man.
The Byzantine capital falls and Greek scholars and manuscripts move west. In Mainz the first printed Bible is completed.
Florence at its most brilliant. He survives an assassination attempt in the cathedral in 1478 in which his brother is killed.
The French invade, the Medici are expelled and a Dominican friar rules Florence, burning vanities in the square until he is burned himself.
Leonardo paints the refectory wall in Milan for Duke Ludovico Sforza.
Michelangelo paints more than three hundred figures on the vault, standing on a scaffold. Raphael is at work in the pope’s rooms next door.
Machiavelli writes his treatise in exile. It is printed in 1532, after his death.
Unpaid troops of Emperor Charles V loot the city for months. Artists scatter across Italy and Europe.
The first history of art is published in Florence and gives the age its name of rebirth.

concepts.detail: A programme of study, not a creed. Its claim was that reading the best ancient authors in their own words forms judgment, eloquence and character.
Parallel lines running away from the viewer are drawn to meet at a single point on the horizon. The picture becomes a window, with the viewer’s eye at a fixed place.
The ideal of a person developed on every side. It rested on the belief that the arts and sciences are connected and that one mind can hold them.
Life is a contest between what happens to us and what we are able to make of it. The able person watches for occasion and seizes it.
Painters worked to written contracts that named the subject, the size, the delivery date and how much blue and gold was to be used.
Artists were to study the visible world directly: bodies, plants, light, weather. Leonardo told painters to carry a notebook and draw people in the street.
Ancient statues, buildings and texts were measured and copied as models of excellence. To be modern was to be like the ancients.

concepts.text: Learning in the service of the republic.
concepts.detail: Florentine chancellors such as Leonardo Bruni argued that the educated citizen owes his talents to public life.
Ficino’s circle taught that love of visible beauty can lead the soul upward to the divine. The idea shaped Botticelli and Michelangelo.

facts.text: Leonardo wrote his notes from right to left in mirror script, probably because he was left-handed and it kept his hand out of the wet ink.
Brunelleschi’s dome contains more than four million bricks and weighs about thirty-seven thousand tons.
The word renaissance was not used in English for the period until the 1830s.
Michelangelo signed only one work, the Pietà in Saint Peter’s, on the band across the Virgin’s chest.
About twenty million books had been printed in Europe by 1500.
Florence had perhaps sixty thousand inhabitants in the fifteenth century, fewer than a small modern town.

sensitivity.note: This Onda borrows the working habits of Renaissance artists and scholars. The picture of a golden age is partly the period’s own invention, and it is worth holding it together with the facts below.
requiredCaveats: The education and the workshops described here were open to very few, and to almost no women. Those who did succeed, like Sofonisba Anguissola, were exceptions made possible by rank.
Italian cities of the time kept slaves, fought constant wars and persecuted Jews, and the same age opened the Atlantic slave trade and the conquest of the Americas.
Greek science and philosophy reached Italy largely through Arab and Byzantine scholars, whose part the humanists played down.
